cards.front: Recall a key point about The Treaty of Versailles
cards.back: The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles, exactly 5 years after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. It was primarily negotiated by three leaders: Wilson (USA), Clemenceau (France), and Lloyd George (Britain). Their conflicting aims made a balanced settlement almost impossible.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Treaty of Versailles
cards.back: The Treaty of Versailles had five main categories: War Guilt, Reparations, Military restrictions, Territorial losses, and the League of Nations. Germans called it the "Diktat" (dictated peace) because they were not allowed to negotiate the terms.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Treaty of Versailles
cards.back: Germany lost 13% of its European territory, 10% of its population, and all of its overseas empire. The "Polish Corridor" was particularly resented because it separated East Prussia from the rest of Germany and placed millions of ethnic Germans under Polish rule.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Treaty of Versailles
cards.back: Germans called the Treaty a "Diktat" (dictated peace) because they were given no opportunity to negotiate. The German delegation was shown the terms on 7 May 1919 and told to sign within 15 days. When they proposed modifications, the Allies rejected all significant changes. The German government initially refused to sign, but agreed after the Allies threatened to invade.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Treaty of Versailles
cards.back: The League of Nations was created as part of the Treaty of Versailles. Wilson's Fourteenth Point called for "a general association of nations" to maintain peace. The League's Covenant (rules) was incorporated into all the peace treaties. However, the US Senate refused to ratify the Treaty, meaning America never joined the League - undermining it from the start.

cards.front: What should you know about history exam tips — the treaty of versailles?
cards.back: 1. For The Treaty of Versailles, include specific factual detail: dates, names, events and statistics where relevant 2. For source questions, analyse provenance (who, when, why, audience) before using the content 3. In evaluation questions, discuss multiple factors and weigh their relative significance 4. Always link back to the question focus — don't just narrate what happened with The Treaty of Versailles 5. Use phrases like 'the most significant factor was... because...' to show analytical judgement
